analysis.one_liner: Designates dozens of California desert wilderness areas, preserves historic back-country trails, and locks in Navy use of desert military lands.
analysis.headline: Introduced in October 1989 with 15 cosponsors, the bill never left two House committees, and the 101st Congress ended in January 1991 without any floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would designate dozens of Bureau of Land Management desert areas in California as wilderness, protecting them from development while preserving grazing, military overflights, and Native American access. It would create a permanent system of eight historic back-country trails kept open to public vehicular travel. It would also reserve about 1.3 million acres — the China Lake Naval Weapons Center and the Chocolate Mountain Aerial Gunnery Range — for Navy weapons testing for 25 years, while keeping those lands open to mining and geothermal leasing under five-year reviews. Everything else already studied for wilderness would be permanently released from wilderness protections, and the Interior Department would be barred from studying those lands again unless Congress acted.
analysis.who_benefits: Hikers, hunters, conservationists, and desert visitors gain permanent protection of large scenic and wildlife areas. Off-road and historic-route travelers gain a protected trails system open year-round. Native American tribes gain guaranteed access for traditional cultural and religious uses, including pine nut harvesting, with the option of temporary closures to protect religious privacy. Grazing permittees and mining claim holders also gain from preserved grazing rights, waived mining-claim reviews, and periodic openings of military-withdrawn lands to mining and geothermal leasing.

how_it_helps.text: Designates dozens of BLM desert areas in California as wilderness, adding them to the National Wilderness Preservation System and shielding them from development.

Creates a California Desert Back Country Trails System of eight historic routes, each open to the public throughout its length every day of the year, preserving public vehicular access to the Mojave Trail, the Bradshaw Trail, the de Anza Trail, and others.

Assures Native Americans nonexclusive access to designated wilderness for traditional cultural and religious purposes, including pine nut harvesting, and allows the Secretary to temporarily close small areas to protect religious privacy at a tribe's request.

Renews the Navy's use of the China Lake and Chocolate Mountain lands for 25 years with annual decontamination reporting and requirements to warn the public and clean up contaminated lands before they are handed back.

analysis.who_pays: Mining claim holders and off-road vehicle users lose access inside the newly designated wilderness areas. Taxpayers bear the cost of managing the new wilderness areas and trails and of funding Navy decontamination on the military lands, since the Navy's cleanup duties apply only 'to the extent funds are made available.' The public also permanently loses the option of future wilderness protection on released lands.
analysis.who_pays_short: Miners, off-road users in wilderness, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill releases every non-designated BLM desert land from wilderness-study protections and bars the Interior Department from ever conducting another wilderness study of those lands unless Congress authorizes one, permanently closing the door on future protection.
Grazing established before enactment continues inside designated wilderness, including motorized vehicle access and maintenance of facilities and water developments.
For 20 years the land agencies are barred from conducting validity examinations of mining claims as a standard procedure inside the new wilderness areas, weakening oversight of claims there.
The United States is held harmless and not liable for injuries or damages from mining, geothermal leasing, or other nonmilitary activity on the withdrawn military lands.

Even while reserved for the Navy, the withdrawn military lands remain open to the Mining Law of 1872 and mineral and geothermal leasing whenever the Interior Secretary determines them suitable, subject only to five-year reviews.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wilderness designations and trail system are real, lasting gains for the public, and the military-land cleanup requirements add accountability. But the bill buys that conservation by making permanent concessions: a no-future-wilderness-study release of the rest of the desert, grazing with motorized access inside wilderness, a 20-year waiver of mining-claim reviews, and liability immunity on military lands. It is a genuine compromise bill — more conservation than its opponents wanted, more industry accommodation than wilderness purists wanted — and its fate shows both sides had reason to let it sit.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees, field hearings were held in California, and then nothing happened — no committee ever reported it, and the 101st Congress ended without a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerry Lewis of California introduced the California Desert Conservation Act of 1989 on October 12, 1989, with 13 original cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to the House committees on Interior and Insular Affairs and Armed Services.

On October 18, 1989, it was sent to the Military Installations and Facilities and Readiness subcommittees, and an executive comment was requested from the Department of Defense; on November 6 it also went to the National Parks and Public Lands subcommittee.
Field hearings were held in Bishop, California (October 28, 1989) and Barstow, California (November 1989) before and after referral.

After the field hearings in November 1989, no further action appears in the record; the bill was never reported out of committee and the 101st Congress ended January 3, 1991 without a House or Senate vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, hardrock mining claim holders, grazing permittees, and off-road vehicle users kept the desert's existing multiple-use arrangement with no new wilderness designations, while the Navy kept operating on its ranges without the new management plan deadlines. Conservationists and wilderness users gained nothing. The California desert was not protected by statute until a later Congress.

for.name: Rep. Jerry Lewis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 13 original cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Armed Services
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to the Military Installations and Facilities and Readiness subcommittees, requested Defense Department comments, and never reported the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to the National Parks and Public Lands subcommittee, but never reported the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided — 12 Republicans and 3 Democrats — and because the bill never received a vote, its party split on the merits was never tested.

industries.note: The bill keeps the China Lake and Chocolate Mountain lands open to the 1872 Mining Law and mineral leasing with five-year suitability reviews, waives validity examinations of wilderness claims for 20 years, but patents convey minerals only, reserving the surface to the United States. Inside the new wilderness areas, new mining is effectively shut out.

Grazing established before enactment continues inside designated wilderness, including motorized access and maintenance of water developments, locking in existing grazing operations on newly protected land.

industries.industry: Off-road vehicle and desert recreation interests
industries.note: Released lands are managed for multiple use rather than held as wilderness study areas, and eight historic trails are kept open year-round for public vehicular travel — a gain shared with ordinary recreationists.

industries.industry: Department of the Navy (weapons testing and training ranges)
industries.note: About 1.3 million acres at China Lake and Chocolate Mountain are reserved for Navy weapons testing and aerial gunnery for 25 years, with Navy authority to close roads to the public, while mineral and geothermal leasing stay open on the same lands; the bill does add decontamination reporting and public-warning duties.
